sections.body: Artificial intelligence in legal work means software that reads documents, drafts clauses, searches case law, and flags risk at a scale no team of lawyers could match by hand. In discovery it sorts millions of files by relevance and privilege before a human ever opens them. In contracts it extracts terms, compares them against playbooks, and proposes redlines. In research it retrieves passages from statutes and opinions and assembles a first draft of a memo. None of this replaces a lawyer's judgment, and the tools still miss context, misread ambiguity, and produce confident errors that a careful reader has to catch.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Document review and contract extraction are the most mature areas, and they work well on high-volume, repetitive material with clear labels. Legal research tools are useful for finding starting points but still fabricate citations and misstate holdings, which is why verification remains mandatory. Prediction of litigation outcomes and judicial behavior is the least reliable, because the data is sparse, outcomes are negotiated rather than adjudicated, and past patterns do not bind future courts. The field is also being reshaped by the law itself: this site tracks 150 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, alongside 29 AI case law precedents, 229 compliance and regulation pages, and 7165 state AI bills, a volume that shows how unsettled the rules remain. The honest limit is that these systems assist and accelerate, they do not decide, and the accountability for a wrong answer still sits with the professional who signed it.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The ten pages divide into the work itself, the rules around it, and the plumbing underneath. E-Discovery and Large-Scale Document Analysis and Contract Lifecycle and Algorithmic Drafting cover the two highest-volume tasks, while Legal Research and Case Strategy and Litigation Prediction and Judicial Analytics address how lawyers find authority and think about outcomes, with the second being the more speculative of the pair. Corporate Governance and Regulatory Compliance and Intellectual Property and Trademark Strategy sit where AI meets institutional obligation and ownership, and Data Privacy and Cyber-Regulatory Compliance handles the data protection duties that run through all of it. Emerging Legal Frameworks is the page for the statutes and cases still being written, and Legal Operations, Infrastructure and Security together with AI Security Audits and Enterprise Enablement cover how firms run these systems and check them. A reader new to the subject should start with discovery and contracts, then move to research and governance, and treat the prediction, frameworks, and audit pages as the places where the open questions live.
